segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: James, a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: greetings.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Consider it all joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you fall into trials of various kinds,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And let endurance have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and whole, lacking in nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all generously and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: double-minded man that he is, unstable in all his ways.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let the lowly brother boast in being raised up,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the rich man in being brought low, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the sun rises with its scorching heat and dries up the grass, and its flower falls and the beauty of its appearance perishes. So too the rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Blessed is the man who endures trial, because once he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let no one say when he is tempted,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am being tempted by God,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But each person is tempted when he is dragged away and lured by his own desire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then desire, having conceived, gives birth to sin, and sin, when it is full-grown, brings forth death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be led astray, my beloved brothers and sisters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every good act of giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow cast by turning.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Know this, my beloved brothers and sisters. Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for a man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, putting away all filth and overflowing wickedness, receive with gentleness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But be doers of the word and not hearers only, deluding yourselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks in a mirror at the face he was born with;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he looks at himself and goes away, and at once forgets what he was like.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one who peers into the perfect law, the law of freedom, and stays with it, becoming not a hearer who forgets but a doer who acts—he will be blessed in his doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone thinks he is religious while not bridling his tongue but deceiving his own heart, that person’s religion is worthless.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to look after orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person who belongs to a master, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way. In the Greek Old Testament “slave of God” or “slave of the Lord” is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and the prophets, so the word conveys both total belonging and dignity. Most English versions have “servant”; some have “slave” or “bondservant.”

“The Dispersion” was the established term for Jews living outside the land of Israel. Whether James is writing to Jewish followers of Jesus in particular, or uses “the twelve tribes” as a picture of the whole church, is debated.
The Greek plural was regularly used for a mixed group of men and women, and James is addressing whole congregations. Many recent translations render it this way; others keep “brothers.”

The word means a putting to the proof, and here it refers to hardships that test whether faith will hold. Older versions have “temptations,” which now suggests enticement to sin; most modern versions have “trials.” The same word returns in verse 12.

The Greek word means complete, fully grown, having reached its goal, and not flawless in the modern sense. Some versions have “mature” or “full effect” here. “Perfect” is kept because James repeats the word in verses 17 and 25, and the repetition appears deliberate.

The adverb’s basic sense is “simply, with singleness of purpose,” and in contexts of giving it shades into “generously.” It may instead mean “without reservation” or “without second thoughts,” which would set God’s single-minded giving against the double-minded asker of verse 8. Both readings have scholarly support.

Standard lexicons give “doubt, waver” for this use of the verb, and almost all translations follow them. Some scholars argue that this sense is not clearly attested outside the New Testament in the period, and that the meaning is closer to “being divided” or “disputing,” that is, being at odds with oneself or with God. The image of the wave and the “double-minded” man in verse 8 fits either reading.

notes.phrase: like a flower of the grass
notes.note: The image and much of the wording of verses 10–11 come from Isaiah 40:6–8 in the Greek Old Testament, where all human glory is like a wildflower that withers while God’s word endures. It is disputed whether “the rich man” here is a fellow believer, with “brother” carried over from verse 9, or an outsider.

The earliest manuscripts have simply “he has promised,” with no subject stated. Later manuscripts add “the Lord” or “God.” “God” is supplied here only because English “he” would be confusing after “the man.”

The verb belongs to the same word-family as “trial” in verses 2 and 12, and its basic meaning is “put to the test.” James moves from outward hardships that test faith to the inward pull toward sin, as the references to evil, desire, and luring show, so “tempt” is used in verses 13–14. Some interpreters keep “test” throughout, reading the point as: no one under trial should blame God for it.

“Lights” means the sun, moon, and stars, and God is called their Father as their creator. The words that follow use the language of astronomy: the heavenly bodies shift and cast changing shadows, but their maker does not change. The wording of the last phrase varies among the manuscripts and its exact sense is uncertain.
The Greek form can be a command (“Know this”) or a statement (“You know this”). Later manuscripts read a different word meaning “so then,” which is what older English versions translate.

“Meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a gentle, humble, unassertive disposition, here set against the anger of verses 19–20. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the usual modern rendering.

The Greek words rendered “religious” and “religion” in verses 26–27 refer to the outward practice of worship—rites, observances, acts of devotion—and not to a system of beliefs. James’s point is that the worship God accepts consists in control of the tongue, care for the vulnerable, and moral integrity.

The verb means to go to see someone out of concern for their welfare, and in the Greek Old Testament it is used of God coming to help his people. “Visit” now suggests a social call, whereas the point here is practical care for people in need. Most versions keep “visit”; some have “look after” or “care for.”

The plural address occurs in nearly every letter, and translators divide between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters”; the singular generic use also needs a consistent policy.
Rendered variously as “patience,” “endurance,” “perseverance,” and “steadfastness” across Paul, Hebrews, James, and Revelation, and should be kept distinct from μακροθυμία.
Versions vary between “perfect,” “mature,” and “complete” in Matthew, Paul, Hebrews, and James, and “perfect” can mislead modern readers into hearing flawlessness.
